definition: A historical philosophical view, associated here with Aristotelian and scholastic thought, that understands nature in terms of causes. In this source it is mentioned as an older framework that Bacon still partly retained in his account of nature.

provenance.revision: 1901 New York Macmillan original; archive index checked 2026-10-18
provenance.scope: Source record Baconian Method; pinned source text

reasons: The packet does not explicitly define the “doctrine of causes” as a view that “understands nature in terms of causes”; it only says Bacon “retains so much of the Aristotelian and scholastic doctrine of causes,” without stating what that doctrine holds in general terms.
The packet only mentions the phrase as part of Bacon’s conception of nature; it does not define the standalone term “doctrine of causes.”

The wording “understands nature in terms of causes” is a broader gloss than the source provides, which only says Bacon’s conception of nature retained “so much of the Aristotelian and scholastic doctrine of causes.”
